title: Full Frontal
full_review:
In the odd ensemble drama "Full Frontal" (Miramax), director Steven Soderbergh hopes to recapture the audience he established with his 1989 "Sex, Lies and Videotape." "Full Frontal" is a decided departure from his big-budgeted blockbuster hits "Erin Brockovich" and "Ocean's Eleven." But this quirky movie is equal parts witty and tedious, following a story line that doesn't bring its disparate parts together satisfactorily.

At times the viewer is absorbed by the situations and events occurring, and in figuring out which is the movie and which is the movie-within-the-movie. It is an experiment in playing with what is and what is not "real" in moviemaking. And the final shot will fool more than a few people in this regard. Soderbergh, once again acting as both director and cameraman (under the pseudonym Peter Andrews), shoots the "real life" of the characters in grainy, reality-style footage over a 24-hour period as the characters cross paths within their small clique of Los Angeles friends and lovers.

Peripheral to the circle is Linda (Mary McCormack), a free-spirited yet neurotic masseuse who fears she will never find true love. Her sister, Lee (Catherine Keener), is an unhappy wife and human resources vice president who takes out her marital frustrations by firing her employees, but not before she cruelly humiliates them behind closed doors. Lee, who is married to sad-sack writer Carl (David Hyde Pierce), is having an affair with Calvin (Blair Underwood), an African-American actor filming a movie in Los Angeles. In this movie, which Soderbergh films in glossy 35mm, Calvin plays Nicholas, an up-and-coming TV star who just got his first big break and is being interviewed by magazine journalist Catherine (Julia Roberts), played by Francesca, the actress (Roberts again). Each of these characters is connected in some way to Gus, a shady Hollywood producer who is celebrating his 40th birthday party in a chic Beverly Hills hotel, which the whole crowd plans to attend that evening.

Sound confusing? This existential head-scratcher is a bit, but Coleman Hough's script is coherent enough up to this point to intrigue the audience without losing their attention in a mishmash of minutiae. However, as the movie continues, flitting back and forth between the Hollywood movie and the documentary-style story of the characters, it begins to lose its appeal. It also becomes evident that Hollywood types and cinema devotees may enjoy it more than others since it is set in
Tinseltown and revolves around the entertainment industry.

The characters reveal themselves to be shallow and self-absorbed, evoking little viewer empathy. The thread that binds them is their individual search for love and acceptance. But each goes about searching for love in wildly different ways. About the only sympathetic character is Carl (played superbly by Pierce), who drags himself to work unaware that his wife, Lee, has left him a note ending their marriage. At work he finds that his career hinges on the hypothetical question of whether he drinks beer straight from the bottle or pours it into a glass. He is the only genuine character in a sea of deceptive individuals who play mind games to achieve their goals.

Enrico Colantoni plays Carl's writing partner and director of "The Sound and the Fuehrer," an "off Broadway" play. Nicky Katt, who plays Hitler in the play, is wildly funny. The character is given the best lines and Katt relishes the opportunity to deliver these zingers.

Before filming began, Soderbergh's set up his own cheeky Dogme 95-like rules for any actor considering a part in "Full Frontal." The actors were required to "pick, provide and maintain" their own wardrobes, as well as "create and maintain" their own hair and makeup. Each needed to provide their own transportation. If they were unable, a driver would pick them up, but they would "probably become the subject of ridicule." And the final of the 10 "rules": You will have fun whether you want to or not. The result is that the cast seemed to invest themselves in the film, but this didn't necessarily translate into fine performances all around.

In their own way, each character is attempting come to terms with their own lives and shortcomings.

Due to a shadowy sexual encounter, brief frontal nudity and drug content, a suicide, an extramarital affair, some sexual references and recurring rough language with some profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.

(
2002
)
